426--- Note to developers:

429---     interacts with the "application" case of `com` and the notation for

434---     `NOTATION: Note for Rocq custom grammar hackers.  From what I can tell, the

436---     strict notion of what counts as "equal" for the purposes of the factorization.
437---     In particular, a grammar entry might have a level,

441---     Hoare triples below includes "at level 99" -- the [LEVEL "99"] part of the
442---     grammar counts for factorization.
443---
444---     The upshot is that means that this notation and the Hoare triple notation
445---     (which overlaps with [{{ _ }}]) must be changed in tandem and use identical
446---     level specifications.`

476-
477--- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
478--- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
479-
480-def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
481-  ∀ st, P st → Q st

492-notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P

501--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
502-
503--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
504--- command. The standard notation is
505-
506---   {P} c {Q}
507-
508--- meaning:
509-
510--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
511--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
512--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
513-
514--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
515--- *postcondition*.
516-
517--- Because single braces are already used for other things in Lean, we'll
518--- write Hoare triples with double braces:
519-
520---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
521-
522--- For example,
523-
524--- - The Hoare triple
525-
526---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
527-
528--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
529--- a state in which `X = 1`.
530-
531--- - On the other hand,
532-
533---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
534-
535--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
536--- `{{X = m}} X :=
537--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
538--- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
539--- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
540-

688-
689--- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
690-
691-def ValidHoareTriple
692-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
693-  ∀ st st',
694-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
695-    P st →
696-    Q st'

698--- Note to developers:
699---     `NOTATION: SAZ 2024 One trickiness of these notations is that we
700---     want the [com] and [assn] grammars to be "open", so that they can
701---     include expressions parsed by the full [constr] grammar of Rocq.
702---     However, then there is a conflict of precedence of the
703---     "application" cases:
704---
705---     The example " {{ True }} X := 0 {{ False }} " does not parse as
706---     intended because the [com] grammar includes the capability of
707---     parsing the (ill-typed) term "0 {{ False }}".
708---
709---     This means that the "application" for [com] should disallow
710---     arguments at the level at which the [assn] grammar is included
711---     in constr.  The upshot is that this notation should be included
712---     in the grammar at the *same* level as the assertion notation
713---     [{{ P }}], which is 2.`

784--- ## Proof Rules
785-
786--- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
787--- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
788--- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
789--- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
790--- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
791--- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
792--- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
793--- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
794--- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
795-
796--- ### Skip
797-
798--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
799-
800---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
801---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
802-
803-theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
804-    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
805-  intro st st' h hp
806-  inversion h
807-  assumption
808-
809--- ### Sequencing
810-
811--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
812--- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
813--- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
814--- where `R` holds:
815-
816---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
817---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
818---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
819---   {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
820-
821-theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
822-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
823-    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{ R }} := by
824-  intro st st' h12 pre
825-  inversion h12 with
826-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
827-    exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
828-
829--- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
830--- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
831--- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
832--- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
833--- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
834--- through commands until we reach the beginning.
835-
836--- ### Assignment
837-
838--- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
839--- rules. Here's how it works.
840-
841--- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
842-
843---   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
844-
845--- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
846--- could the precondition be?
847-
848--- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
849--- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
850-
851---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
852-
853--- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
854--- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
855--- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
856--- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
857--- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
858-
859--- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
860-
861---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
862-
863--- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
864--- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
865-
866---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
867-
868--- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
869--- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
870--- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
871--- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
872--- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
873--- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
874--- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
875-
876--- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
877--- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
878--- expression `a`:
879-
880---   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
881-
882--- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
883--- replaced by `a`.
884-
885--- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
886--- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
887-
888--- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
889-
890---   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
891-
892--- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to

581+-- ### Assertion Implication
582+
583+-- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
584+-- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
585+
586+def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
587+  ∀ st, P st → Q st
588+
589+-- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
590+-- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
591+
592+notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
593+
594+theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
595+
596+-- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
597+
598+notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
599+
600+theorem assertIff_def {P Q : Assertion} : P <<->> Q ↔ AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
601+    := by rfl
602+

604+-- assertions back in `->>` and `<<->>` notation.

633+-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
634+
635+-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
636+-- command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in this
637+-- book, is
638+
639+--   {{P}} c {{Q}}
640+
641+-- meaning:
642+
643+-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
644+-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
645+-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
646+
647+-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
648+-- *postcondition*.
649+
650+-- For example,
651+
652+-- - The Hoare triple
653+
654+--   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
655+
656+-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
657+-- a state in which `X = 1`.
658+
659+-- - On the other hand,
660+
661+--   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
662+
663+-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
664+-- `{{X = m}} X :=
665+-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
666+-- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
667+-- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
668+
669+-- _Quiz:_
670+
671+-- Paraphrase the following in English.
672+
673+--   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
674+
675+--   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
676+
677+--   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
678+
679+--   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
680+
681+--   5) ∀ m,
682+--        {{X = m}}
683+--        c
684+--        {{Y = real_fact m}}
685+
686+--   6) ∀ m,
687+--        {{X = m}}
688+--        c
689+--        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
690+
691+-- _Quiz:_
692+
693+-- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
694+-- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
695+
696+--   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
697+
698+-- (A) Yes
699+
700+-- (B) No
701+
702+-- _Quiz:_
703+
704+-- What about this one?
705+
706+--   {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
707+
708+-- (A) Yes
709+
710+-- (B) No
711+
712+-- _Quiz:_
713+
714+-- What about this one?
715+
716+--   {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
717+
718+-- (A) Yes
719+
720+-- (B) No
721+
722+-- _Quiz:_
723+
724+-- What about this one?
725+
726+--   {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
727+
728+-- (A) Yes
729+
730+-- (B) No
731+
732+-- _Quiz:_
733+
734+-- What about this one?
735+
736+--   {{True}} skip {{False}}
737+
738+-- (A) Yes
739+
740+-- (B) No
741+
742+-- _Quiz:_
743+
744+-- What about this one?
745+
746+--   {{False}} skip {{True}}
747+
748+-- (A) Yes
749+
750+-- (B) No

752+-- _Quiz:_

754+-- What about this one?

815+-- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
816+
817+-- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
818+
819+open scoped HasEval
820+
821+def ValidHoareTriple
822+    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
823+  ∀ {st st' : State},
824+    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
825+    P st →
826+    Q st'
827+
828+-- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
829+--     Somethings strange is going on in `theorem if_example`, using
830+--     `apply hoare_consequence_pre` followed by `· exact hoare_asgn` works,
831+--     but `refine hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn ?_` or
832+--     `apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn` don't. The only solution I
833+--     found was to mark `ValidHoareTriple` irreducible.
834+--
835+--     It has to do something with `apply` and `refine` looking inside the
836+--     implication in `∀ {st st'}, ...`
837+
838+-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
839+-- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
840+-- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
841+-- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
842+
843+class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
844+  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
845+
846+namespace HasTriple
847+
848+/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
849+scoped notation:lead "{{" P "}} " c:lead " {{" Q "}}" => Triple ({{ P }}) c ({{ Q }})
850+
851+/-- Hoare triple with `imp_com` command syntax -/
852+scoped syntax:lead (priority := high) "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
853+scoped macro_rules
854+  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
855+      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
856+end HasTriple
857+
858+instance : HasTriple Com where
859+  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
860+
861+open scoped HasTriple
862+
863+theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
864+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
865+      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
866+      P st →
867+      Q st' := by rfl
868+
869+attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
870+
871+-- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing triples back
872+
873+-- The delaborator is agnostic to the command type: it prints the command with
874+-- whatever printer is registered for its constructors and splices the result
875+-- into the triple, so a language-extension chapter only has to register a
876+-- printer for its own `Com`.
877+
878+namespace Assertion.Delab
879+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
880+@[delab app.HasTriple.Triple]
881+def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
882+  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasTriple.Triple 5
883+  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
884+  let c ← withNaryArg 3 delab
885+  let Q ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssn
886+  match c with
887+  | `(imp { $c:imp_com }) => ``({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
888+  | c => ``({{ $P }} ~$c {{ $Q }})
889+
890+end Assertion.Delab
891+
892+-- END DETAILS

897+-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_post_true ⭐
898+
899+-- Prove that if `Q` holds in every state, then any triple with `Q` as its
900+-- postcondition is valid.
901+
902+theorem hoare_post_true {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
903+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
904+  all_goals
905+    rw [validHoareTriple_def]
906+    intro st st' hc hpre
907+    exact h st'
908+
909+-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false ⭐
910+
911+-- Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with `P` as its
912+-- precondition is valid.
913+
914+theorem hoare_pre_false {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
915+    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
916+  all_goals
917+    rw [validHoareTriple_def]
918+    intro st st' hc hpre
919+    specialize h st
920+    contradiction
921+
922+-- ## Proof Rules
923+
924+-- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
925+-- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
926+-- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
927+-- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
928+-- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
929+-- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
930+-- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
931+-- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
932+-- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
933+
934+-- ### Skip
935+
936+-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
937+
938+--   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
939+--   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
940+
941+theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
942+    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
943+  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
944+  intro st st' h hpre
945+  inversion h
946+  exact hpre
947+
948+-- ### Sequencing
949+
950+-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
951+-- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
952+-- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
953+-- where `R` holds:
954+
955+--    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
956+--    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
957+--   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
958+--   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
959+
960+theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
961+    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
962+    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
963+  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
964+  intro st st' h hpre
965+  inversion h with
966+  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
967+    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
968+    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
969+
970+-- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
971+-- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
972+-- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
973+-- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
974+-- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
975+-- through commands until we reach the beginning.
976+
977+-- ### Assignment
978+
979+-- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
980+-- rules. Here's how it works.
981+
982+-- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
983+
984+--   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
985+
986+-- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
987+-- could the precondition be?
988+
989+-- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
990+-- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
991+
992+--   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
993+
994+-- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
995+-- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
996+-- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
997+-- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
998+-- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
999+
1000+-- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
1001+
1002+--   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1003+
1004+-- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
1005+-- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
1006+
1007+--   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1008+
1009+-- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
1010+-- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
1011+-- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
1012+-- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
1013+-- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
1014+-- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
1015+-- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
1016+
1017+-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
1018+-- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
1019+-- expression `a`:
1020+
1021+--   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1022+
1023+-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
1024+-- replaced by `a`.
1025+
1026+-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
1027+-- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
1028+
1029+-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
1030+
1031+--   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1032+
1033+-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
1034+-- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
1035+-- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
1036+-- for every occurrence of `X`.
1037+
1038+-- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
1039+-- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
1040+-- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
1041+-- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
1042+
1043+-- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
1044+-- We'll do that later in some exercises.
1045+
1046+-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
1047+
1048+--   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
1049+--     X := X + 1
1050+--   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1051+
1052+--   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
1053+--     X := 3
1054+--   {{ X = 3 }}
1055+
1056+--   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
1057+--     X := 3
1058+--   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
1059+
1060+-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
1061+-- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
1062+-- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
1063+
1064+-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
1065+-- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
1066+-- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
1067+
1068+-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
1069+-- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
1070+-- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
1071+-- directly "edit" its text.
1072+
1073+-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
1074+-- state, defined as follows:
1075+
1076+def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
1077+  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
1078+
1079+-- Note to developers (One An @meluge, before next release):
1080+--     Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)
1081+
1082+namespace Assertion
1083+
1084+/-- Assertion substitution, written inside the braces: `{{ (P) [X ↦ a] }}`.
1085+The substituted assertion is re-read with the same notation, so Imp
1086+variables in it mean state lookups as usual; a named assertion is passed
1087+through directly. -/
1088+scoped syntax:max term:arg " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
1089+
1090+macro_rules
1091+  | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a:imp_aexp])) =>
1092+    match P with
1093+    | `($_:ident) => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) $P $st)
1094+    | _ => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}) $st)
1095+
1096+theorem subst_def {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} :
1097+    Assertion.subst x a P = fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
1098+
1099+@[simp]
1100+theorem subst_apply {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} {st : State} :
1101+    Assertion.subst x a P st ↔ P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
1102+
1103+end Assertion

1138+-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
1139+-- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
1140+-- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.

1144+-- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression

1170+-- X + 1]`.

1185+--     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1186+

250--- We make it a little easier to write Imp programs using normal constructors
251--- (i.e., without notation), by using *implicit coercions*. In Lean, a `Coe`
252--- instance tells the elaborator how to turn a value of one type into another
253--- automatically:
254-
255--- - `Coe Ident Aexp` lets us write a bare variable (an `Ident`) where an `Aexp`
256---   is expected; the identifier is implicitly wrapped with `id`.
257-
258--- - `OfNat Aexp n` lets us write a numeric literal where an `Aexp` is expected;
259---   it is implicitly wrapped with `num`.
260-
261--- - `Coe Bool Bexp` lets us write a boolean literal (`true`/`false`) where a
262---   `Bexp` is expected; it is implicitly wrapped with `bool`.

383+namespace Algebra
384+
385+-- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to define
386+-- mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about how those
387+-- operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a
388+-- *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
389+
390+-- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
391+
392+-- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
393+--   elements of type `α` into one,
394+
395+-- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
396+--   element", and
397+
398+-- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
399+
400+--   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
401+--   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is associative)
402+
403+-- We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
404+
405+-- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
406+class OpSet (α : Type) where
407+  op : α → α → α
408+
409+infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
410+
411+class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
412+  id : α
413+  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
414+  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
415+  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
416+
417+-- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
418+-- `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
419+-- notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`,
420+-- similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
421+
422+-- As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where `0`
423+-- is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet`
424+-- instance separately, we can define a single instance that implements both
425+-- classes.
426+
427+instance : Monoid Nat where
428+  op := Nat.add
429+  id := 0
430+  left_id := by lia
431+  right_id := by lia
432+  assoc := by lia
433+
434+-- ### Exercise (1 star): NatMonoidMul ⭐
435+
436+-- However, multiplication on `Nat`s *also* forms a monoid. What is its
437+-- identity element?
438+
439+instance : Monoid Nat where
440+  op := Nat.mul
441+  id := (1)
442+  left_id := (by lia)
443+  right_id := (by lia)
444+  assoc := (by lia)
445+
446+-- ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
447+
448+-- There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully in computer
449+-- science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as the
450+-- operator in question:
451+
452+instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
453+  op := List.append
454+  id := ([])
455+  left_id := (by simp)
456+  right_id := (by simp)
457+  assoc := (by simp)
458+
459+-- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
460+-- properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on the
461+-- typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity element of
462+-- a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set with
463+-- the same operator, their identity elements must also be the same:
464+
465+theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
466+  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
467+  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
468+  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
469+    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
470+    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
471+    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
472+    rw [h]
473+    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
474+    rw [right_id₂]
475+  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
476+  exact h'
477+
478+-- In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and `m₂`
479+-- with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do so
480+-- however, because these are class instances instead of normal structures, we
481+-- preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above
482+-- proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can set
483+-- `set_option pp.all true` or `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show
484+-- you more clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
485+-- `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
486+-- arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
487+-- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
488+
489+-- A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation `inv`,
490+-- which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`. We can
491+-- extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
492+
493+class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
494+  inv : α → α
495+  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
496+  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
497+
498+-- Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups: there is no inverse
499+-- operation on the natural numbers such that
500+-- `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However, addition does form
501+-- a group over the integers:
502+
503+-- ### Exercise (1 star): IntGroupAdd ⭐
504+
505+instance : Group Int where
506+  op := Int.add
507+  id := (0)
508+  inv := (Int.neg)
509+  left_id := (by lia)
510+  right_id := (by lia)
511+  assoc := (by lia)
512+  left_inv := (by lia)
513+  right_inv := (by lia)
514+
515+-- The study of groups is called *group theory* and is a rich area of
516+-- mathematics. Here, we will only prove a handful of its simplest results:
517+
518+-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
519+--     This also prints weird.
520+
521+-- ### Exercise (1 star): InverseUnique ⭐
522+
523+-- Two groups defined with the same operation over the same set must have the
524+-- same inverse as well.
525+
526+theorem inv_unique {α : Type} {g₁ g₂ : Group α} (h : g₁.op = g₂.op) : g₁.inv = g₂.inv := by
527+  all_goals
528+    ext a
529+    rw [←g₁.right_id (Group.inv a), ←g₁.right_inv a]
530+    rw [g₁.assoc, h, g₂.left_inv a, g₂.left_id]
531+
532+-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
533+--     Taking suggestions for additional simple group theory theorems to prove
534+--     here.
535+
536+end Algebra
537+
